extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting papers to NeurIPS (machine learning researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: The NeurIPS Paper Checklist: a set of transparency, reproducibility, ethics, and impact questions authors should answer (yes/no/n/a) and reference within their submission. It guides what to include in papers, supplements, and released assets to help reviewers evaluate reproducibility, societal impact, and ethical compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist answers and referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: You should answer yes, no, or n/a. You should reference the section(s) of the paper that provide support for your answer. You can also optionally write a short (1–2 sentence) justification of your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although 'yes' is generally preferable, answering 'no' is acceptable with proper justification (e.g., computational expense, unavailable license). Supporting evidence can appear in the main paper or supplemental material. Reviewers will use the checklist as one factor in evaluation. Use best judgement; the true answers are often nuanced, so add justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main claims reflect contributions and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper's contributions and scope?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should match theoretical and experimental results in terms of expected generalization. Contributions should be clearly stated along with important assumptions and limitations. Aspirational goals may be included but must be clearly labelled as not attained by the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with ethics review guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you read the ethics review guidelines and ensured that your paper conforms to them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should read the linked ethics review guidelines and ensure compliance; this question is a prompt to check for ethical issues per NeurIPS policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion of potential negative societal impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you discuss any potential negative societal impacts of your work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, surveillance), environmental impact (training huge models), fairness, privacy, and security. Consider harms when used as intended, when giving incorrect results, and from misuse. Consider stakeholders, especially vulnerable or marginalized communities. If harms exist, discuss mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release, defenses, monitoring). Examples and external guidance are provided (unofficial guidance, broader impacts workshop resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you describe the limitations of your work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraged to create a separate 'Limitations' section. Point out strong assumptions and robustness to violations (e.g., independence, noiseless settings), reflect on scope of claims (datasets, number of runs), and factors influencing performance (e.g., image resolution, lighting). Honesty is encouraged and reviewers are instructed not to penalize truthful limitation statements; avoid hiding limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical results: state full assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you state the full set of assumptions of all theoretical results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in theorem statements. Discuss relationship to related literature where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical results: include complete proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you include complete proofs of all theoretical results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs can appear in the main paper or supplemental material; if in supplement, provide a short proof sketch in the main paper to provide intuition. Encourage discussion of relationships to related results in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility: provide code, data, and instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you include the code, data, and instructions needed to reproduce the main experimental results (either in the supplemental material or as a URL)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run and reproduce results. Main experiments include new method and baselines; try to capture as many minor experiments as possible and state which ones are reproducible. At submission time, preserve anonymity by releasing anonymized versions. 'No because code is proprietary' is an acceptable answer if justified. See NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental details: training and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you specify all the training details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full details can be in the code, but important details should be in the main paper. Include how hyperparameters were chosen and data split specifications so experiments are interpretable and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental uncertainty: report error bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you report error bars (e.g., with respect to the random seed after running experiments multiple times)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer 'yes' if you report error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests for your main experiments. These quantify variability (e.g., random seeds) and support claims about performance differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute and resource reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you include the amount of compute and the type of resources used (e.g., type of GPUs, internal cluster, or cloud provider)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally provide compute required for individual experimental runs as well as total compute. State types of hardware (GPUs, clusters) used. Encouraged to use CO2 emissions trackers (experiment impact tracker, ML CO2 impact calculator, CodeCarbon) and report environmental impact if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite creators of existing assets
rubrics_metrics.description: If your work uses existing assets, did you cite the creators?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. State which version of the asset you're using and include a URL if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: State license for assets used
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you mention the license of the assets?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the license name (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) for each asset. If you scraped data from a source, state the copyright and terms of service. For popular datasets, check paperswithcode.com/datasets and their licensing guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: License and terms for released assets
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are releasing assets, did you include a license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear licensing and terms for any released assets. This applies to code, datasets, and derived assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repackaged datasets: state original and derived licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are repackaging an existing dataset, did you state the original license as well as the one for the derived asset (if it has changed)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about licensing changes when repackaging or modifying datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: When license is unknown, contact creators
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot find license information online, did you reach out to the asset's creators?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are encouraged to try to determine licensing by contacting original creators when information isn't publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include new assets and anonymize at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you include any new assets either in the supplemental material or as a URL?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including new assets at submission, remember to anonymize them (anonymized URL or anonymized zip file). If assets cannot be released (e.g., proprietary), state the reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent for data involving people
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose data you're using/curating?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For collected data (e.g., crowdsourcing), explain how instructions to participants explained use of data. For existing datasets, check how data was collected and whether consent was obtained; acknowledge this may be difficult but make best effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of PII or offensive content in data
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you discuss whether the data you are using/curating contains personally identifiable information or offensive content?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how you checked for PII or offensive content (e.g., sampling scripts, manual checks). Note that presence of such content is not necessarily bad, but should be disclosed and discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human subjects: include full instructions and screenshots
rubrics_metrics.description: If you used crowdsourcing or conducted research with human subjects, did you include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including this information in supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution involves human subjects, include as much detail as possible in the main paper to enable evaluation and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human subjects: describe participant risks and IRB status
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you describe any potential participant risks, with links to Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals, if applicable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of risks include exposure to offensive content or collection of PII. If IRB approval was obtained, state this in the paper; for initial submissions, do not include information that breaks anonymity (e.g., institution name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human subjects: report participant compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you include the estimated hourly wage paid to participants and the total amount spent on participant compensation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the amount paid for each task (including bonuses), discuss how task duration was estimated, and how the wage was determined to be fair.
